Tools search and summarize it directly; query_sql is available for anything else.

Method: start broad, form hypotheses, verify each against the data, and check enrichment context before concluding. Cite every malicious event you rely on by its audit event ID. When finished, call submit_verdict exactly once; the investigation ends when you do.

input.summary: Someone used Jordan Doe's (jdoe@example.com) credentials to attack payments-prod. Jordan is on PTO (2026-10-12..19) and normally uses darwin, but every one of these requests came from linux kubectl at 198.51.100.23. That IP belongs to NIGHTOWL-HOSTING (NL), is rated malicious and is tagged bulletproof hosting, k8s API brute-force and an open Docker registry on port 5000. The same 14-step playbook ran on EKS (14:02-14:25), GKE (14:38-15:01) and AKS (15:11-15:34): check permissions, list namespaces, fail to read kube-system secrets and create a kube-system job, then list payments secrets and read payments-db-credentials. Next it started a privileged alpine pod (debug-tools-7f9c, hostPID, host root mounted, not allowlisted) and exec'd nsenter into the node's PID 1 to break out to the host. Using the argocd-application-controller service-account token (cluster-admin) from the same outside IP, it created the ClusterRoleBinding 'jdoe-break-glass', which gives Jordan's identity cluster-admin. With that it planted persistence: DaemonSet kube-system/kube-metrics-agent pulling 198.51.100.23:5000/metrics-agent:latest, CronJob kube-system/node-cert-rotate and Service default/metrics-agent-np. It finished with a cluster-wide secrets dump (the alert). All three clouds are affected, including PCI-classified prod data: payments DB credentials and every secret in all namespaces should be treated as stolen, along with the argocd SA tokens and Jordan's credentials on AWS, GCP and Azure.
